Physical identity and semantic decision: the final category is vegetation because dedicated family planter resolves the physical object as vegetation. Model it as a botanically or ecologically coherent plant, tree, crop, coral, fungus, or landscaped growth asset with believable anchoring and growth hierarchy. Words describing an animal, profession, customer, owner, district, collection, or story function may not force character or creature anatomy onto an object such as a cottage, boat, crate, display, station, rack, board, feeder, machine, sign, or piece of equipment. The named object must be identifiable in neutral clay material before labels, color, and glow are applied.

Silhouette and proportion: Species category and maturity must read from trunk, stem, branch rhythm, crown, leaf massing, roots, fronds, petals, coral arms, fungal caps, or planting container. Keep the working envelope near 1 meters wide, 1 meters deep, and 0.75 meters high. Only reviewed protrusions such as signs, arms, doors, mirrors, roots, branches, railings, hoses, lighting, propulsion, awnings, stairs, or service hardware may extend beyond it. Every major and secondary form must reinforce Dreamdrop Community Garden Bed; unrelated decorative mass should be removed.

Construction and functional anatomy: Build a clear hierarchy from roots or anchor through trunk, branches, stems, leaves, flowers, fruit, coral polyps, or other species structures rather than spheres or disconnected cards. Required visible components are outer planter body, inner soil volume, rim, drainage detail, planting. Each one must connect through credible frames, joints, seams, foundations, roots, brackets, fasteners, cables, pipes, glazing frames, hinges, biological attachment, serving structure, packaging, or material transitions. Flat paint, decals, and emission may not replace a component that explains operation, weight support, access, occupancy, growth, containment, drainage, power, preparation, protection, or maintenance.

Materials, color, and lighting: use the named material vocabulary painted metal, concrete, ordinary glass, galvanized hardware, warm brick, cream, storefront blue, civic navy, school green, utility gray, residential sage. welcoming, lived-in American city realism; warm brick, stucco, concrete, patched asphalt, painted metal, ordinary civic and residential materials. Metal surfaces need distinct painted, powder-coated, galvanized, brushed, cast, polished, oxidized, or heat-affected responses rather than one universal gray material. Glass requires thickness, framing, tint appropriate to the town, controlled transparency, believable roughness, and an interior or backing surface so it does not read as an empty blue plane. Stone, brick, concrete, plaster, stucco, tile, and asphalt should show scale-correct joints, aggregate or surface breakup, edge wear, drainage staining, and construction transitions without noisy procedural speckling. Wood needs believable board direction, grain scale, end grain, joinery, sealing, wear, and moisture response appropriate to indoor, residential, marine, fantasy, or industrial use. Fabric, upholstery, leather, rubber, and flexible polymers require thickness, seams, compression or tension cues, stitching where visible, and roughness variation tied to handling. Emissive accents must arise from a lens, strip, screen, projector, fixture, biological organ, or energy component. Do not paint unexplained neon lines across ordinary structure. Avoid the town-specific failures: citywide neon wash, toy-town proportions, sterile empty streets. Surface variation should follow manufacturing, age, handling, weather, moisture, heat, pressure, preparation, cleaning, or maintenance rather than random noise. Emissive areas must originate from a real lens, screen, fixture, projector, biological organ, or energy system.

Condition and environmental integration: Apply restrained lived-in wear at contact points, lower edges, hinges, handles, feet, fasteners, drainage paths, service openings, tires, exposed corners, or frequently cleaned surfaces. Match the district’s maintenance level rather than using uniform dirt or uniform perfection. Anchor it in soil, rock, a planter, cultivated bed, roof garden, seabed, coral substrate, wall pocket, or shoreline appropriate to the species. Root or attachment structure, growth direction, density, wind or current response, and navigation clearance must fit the environment. Add contact shadows, foundations, feet, brackets, roots, piles, seals, trim, drainage, terrain blending, waterline response, or wall transitions where the object meets its environment. It may not appear pasted into the scene or suspended by invisible support unless the design explicitly includes a justified force, mount, cable, lift field, or suspension system.

Interaction and state design: Provide wind groups, harvest points, breakable regions, climbable trunks, collision roots, seasonal variants, and placement sockets where gameplay requires them. Expected hooks include seating, occupancy, or interaction sockets, wind, current, harvest, damage, growth, season, or placement-variation groups. Separate and name parts that can open, slide, rotate, illuminate, display content, receive an item, carry an occupant, change material, emit particles, take damage, be repaired, be harvested, or connect to another system. Static detail should remain efficient, but useful gameplay state boundaries may not be merged away.

Collision, orientation, and export: Use trunk, major branch, root, planter, coral-anchor, or harvest collision only where gameplay needs blocking, climbing, damage, or collection. Leaves, petals, grass blades, and small fronds remain nonblocking. Use positive Z as the front or primary use direction and positive Y as up after export conversion. Place the origin at the ground contact, wall mount, suspension point, waterline, or logical placement center. Use one named asset root, semantically named render meshes, separate animated or stateful parts, simplified collision, and metadata for asset ID, town, family, source document, license, dimensions, final semantic category, and specification version. Remove preview cameras, lights, helpers, unused materials, duplicates, hidden placeholders, and accidental geometry before GLB export.

Performance and LOD: Use clusters, cards, instances, and impostors strategically while preserving species silhouette and branching logic and controlling overdraw. Close-range output may use up to the reviewed maximum, with a practical target near 12,480 triangles when silhouette and required components justify it. Medium-range output should target roughly 5,760 triangles while preserving primary form, supports, interaction components, openings, material blocks, and essential lights. Far output should target roughly 1,920 triangles or a suitable impostor while retaining the recognizable outline, mounting or ground relationship, and major color or emissive signature. Reduction may never destroy this recognition requirement: Species category and maturity must read from trunk, stem, branch rhythm, crown, leaf massing, roots, fronds, petals, coral arms, fungal caps, or planting container.

Acceptance standard: the final model must look intentional from every inspection angle, satisfy every required component, fit the reviewed scale, use meaningful material separation, remain inside geometry budgets, sit correctly on its placement plane, and export as a verified nonempty GLB. A technically valid file that looks generic, toy-like, structurally impossible, context-free, semantically misclassified, or unlike Dreamdrop Community Garden Bed is a failure. Correct it, retry it, or quarantine it instead of publishing it.

assets.deepDescription:
Starter Industrial Dumpster is the definitive production specification for prop_starter_industrial_dumpster_a_v01.glb in starter-town. It originates from docs/STARTER_TOWN_BLUEPRINT.md under “F. Industrial filler.” A production-ready Starter Industrial Dumpster, designed as a public trash receptacle for Starter Town. Show how waste enters, how sanitation workers empty it, and how the receptacle remains stable outdoors. The object must remain immediately recognizable from silhouette and required components, use physically coherent construction and human or vehicle scale, and follow the town direction: welcoming, lived-in American city realism; warm brick, stucco, concrete, patched asphalt, painted metal, ordinary civic and residential materials. This asset appears under the blueprint section “F. Industrial filler” and should visibly support that gameplay or environmental role rather than acting as generic filler. The blueprint evidence is: D. Commercial filler E. Civic and school filler F. Industrial filler

Physical identity and semantic decision: the final category is infrastructure because dedicated family municipal_trash_can resolves the physical object as infrastructure. Model it as a serviceable civic, industrial, marine, utility, transit, security, or public-realm asset whose installation, operation, protection, and maintenance logic are visible. Words describing an animal, profession, customer, owner, district, collection, or story function may not force character or creature anatomy onto an object such as a cottage, boat, crate, display, station, rack, board, feeder, machine, sign, or piece of equipment. The named object must be identifiable in neutral clay material before labels, color, and glow are applied.

Silhouette and proportion: Recognition must come from the relationship between support, enclosure, operating surface, access point, protected hardware, and ground, wall, dock, road, or network connection. Keep the working envelope near 0.72 meters wide, 0.72 meters deep, and 1.15 meters high. Only reviewed protrusions such as signs, arms, doors, mirrors, roots, branches, railings, hoses, lighting, propulsion, awnings, stairs, or service hardware may extend beyond it. Every major and secondary form must reinforce Starter Industrial Dumpster; unrelated decorative mass should be removed.

Construction and functional anatomy: Include mounting, foundations or brackets, structural members, weather or pressure protection, access, hinges, latches, vents, conduit or cable paths, drainage, warnings, controls, and maintenance hardware as appropriate. Required visible components are liner, outer enclosure, support rings, disposal opening, rain cover, service access, base anchors. Each one must connect through credible frames, joints, seams, foundations, roots, brackets, fasteners, cables, pipes, glazing frames, hinges, biological attachment, serving structure, packaging, or material transitions. Flat paint, decals, and emission may not replace a component that explains operation, weight support, access, occupancy, growth, containment, drainage, power, preparation, protection, or maintenance.

Materials, color, and lighting: use the named material vocabulary painted metal, concrete, ordinary glass, galvanized hardware, warm brick, cream, storefront blue, civic navy, school green, utility gray, residential sage. welcoming, lived-in American city realism; warm brick, stucco, concrete, patched asphalt, painted metal, ordinary civic and residential materials. Metal surfaces need distinct painted, powder-coated, galvanized, brushed, cast, polished, oxidized, or heat-affected responses rather than one universal gray material. Glass requires thickness, framing, tint appropriate to the town, controlled transparency, believable roughness, and an interior or backing surface so it does not read as an empty blue plane. Stone, brick, concrete, plaster, stucco, tile, and asphalt should show scale-correct joints, aggregate or surface breakup, edge wear, drainage staining, and construction transitions without noisy procedural speckling. Wood needs believable board direction, grain scale, end grain, joinery, sealing, wear, and moisture response appropriate to indoor, residential, marine, fantasy, or industrial use. Fabric, upholstery, leather, rubber, and flexible polymers require thickness, seams, compression or tension cues, stitching where visible, and roughness variation tied to handling. Emissive accents must arise from a lens, strip, screen, projector, fixture, biological organ, or energy component. Do not paint unexplained neon lines across ordinary structure. Avoid the town-specific failures: citywide neon wash, toy-town proportions, sterile empty streets. Surface variation should follow manufacturing, age, handling, weather, moisture, heat, pressure, preparation, cleaning, or maintenance rather than random noise. Emissive areas must originate from a real lens, screen, fixture, projector, biological organ, or energy system.

Condition and environmental integration: Apply restrained lived-in wear at contact points, lower edges, hinges, handles, feet, fasteners, drainage paths, service openings, tires, exposed corners, or frequently cleaned surfaces. Match the district’s maintenance level rather than using uniform dirt or uniform perfection. Install it on the named ground, curb, wall, road, dock, roof, utility corridor, platform, shoreline, or service foundation. Show anchors, brackets, conduits, piles, seals, drainage, clearance, and maintenance access so the device belongs to a real network rather than floating as decoration. Add contact shadows, foundations, feet, brackets, roots, piles, seals, trim, drainage, terrain blending, waterline response, or wall transitions where the object meets its environment. It may not appear pasted into the scene or suspended by invisible support unless the design explicitly includes a justified force, mount, cable, lift field, or suspension system.

Interaction and state design: Separate controls, doors, lenses, lights, handles, hoses, nozzles, movable arms, covers, gates, scanners, cameras, and service components so systems can animate or change state. Expected hooks include transform, material-state, damage, pickup, or placement hook only where gameplay requires it. Separate and name parts that can open, slide, rotate, illuminate, display content, receive an item, carry an occupant, change material, emit particles, take damage, be repaired, be harvested, or connect to another system. Static detail should remain efficient, but useful gameplay state boundaries may not be merged away.

Collision, orientation, and export: Use one or more primitive or low-complexity hulls matching the major blocking volume and interaction surface. Decorative handles, cables, slats, fasteners, trim, lenses, foliage, and surface detail must not create snagging collision. Use positive Z as the front or primary use direction and positive Y as up after export conversion. Place the origin at the ground contact, wall mount, suspension point, waterline, or logical placement center. Use one named asset root, semantically named render meshes, separate animated or stateful parts, simplified collision, and metadata for asset ID, town, family, source document, license, dimensions, final semantic category, and specification version. Remove preview cameras, lights, helpers, unused materials, duplicates, hidden placeholders, and accidental geometry before GLB export.

Performance and LOD: Preserve functional outline, installation, and operating surfaces. Repeated bolts, louvers, bars, lenses, posts, and rails should use instancing, while collision follows major volumes. Close-range output may use up to the reviewed maximum, with a practical target near 15,600 triangles when silhouette and required components justify it. Medium-range output should target roughly 7,200 triangles while preserving primary form, supports, interaction components, openings, material blocks, and essential lights. Far output should target roughly 2,400 triangles or a suitable impostor while retaining the recognizable outline, mounting or ground relationship, and major color or emissive signature. Reduction may never destroy this recognition requirement: Recognition must come from the relationship between support, enclosure, operating surface, access point, protected hardware, and ground, wall, dock, road, or network connection.

Acceptance standard: the final model must look intentional from every inspection angle, satisfy every required component, fit the reviewed scale, use meaningful material separation, remain inside geometry budgets, sit correctly on its placement plane, and export as a verified nonempty GLB. A technically valid file that looks generic, toy-like, structurally impossible, context-free, semantically misclassified, or unlike Starter Industrial Dumpster is a failure. Correct it, retry it, or quarantine it instead of publishing it.

The named object must be identifiable in neutral clay material before labels, color, and glow are applied.

Silhouette and proportion: The primary body and functional secondary parts must identify the object before labels or color. Handles, supports, openings, controls, edges, and contact points should explain use. Keep the working envelope near 1.5 meters wide, 1.5 meters deep, and 1.5 meters high. Only reviewed protrusions such as signs, arms, doors, mirrors, roots, branches, railings, hoses, lighting, propulsion, awnings, stairs, or service hardware may extend beyond it. Every major and secondary form must reinforce Starter Retaining Wall; unrelated decorative mass should be removed.

Construction and functional anatomy: Model the load-bearing body, panels, seams, hinges, fasteners, supports, handles, vents, feet, brackets, openings, service access, and functional hardware appropriate to the object. Required visible components are recognizable primary structure, functional secondary components, appropriate materials. Each one must connect through credible frames, joints, seams, foundations, roots, brackets, fasteners, cables, pipes, glazing frames, hinges, biological attachment, serving structure, packaging, or material transitions. Flat paint, decals, and emission may not replace a component that explains operation, weight support, access, occupancy, growth, containment, drainage, power, preparation, protection, or maintenance.

Materials, color, and lighting: use the named material vocabulary painted metal, concrete, ordinary glass, galvanized hardware, warm brick, cream, storefront blue, civic navy, school green, utility gray, residential sage. welcoming, lived-in American city realism; warm brick, stucco, concrete, patched asphalt, painted metal, ordinary civic and residential materials. Metal surfaces need distinct painted, powder-coated, galvanized, brushed, cast, polished, oxidized, or heat-affected responses rather than one universal gray material. Glass requires thickness, framing, tint appropriate to the town, controlled transparency, believable roughness, and an interior or backing surface so it does not read as an empty blue plane. Stone, brick, concrete, plaster, stucco, tile, and asphalt should show scale-correct joints, aggregate or surface breakup, edge wear, drainage staining, and construction transitions without noisy procedural speckling. Wood needs believable board direction, grain scale, end grain, joinery, sealing, wear, and moisture response appropriate to indoor, residential, marine, fantasy, or industrial use. Fabric, upholstery, leather, rubber, and flexible polymers require thickness, seams, compression or tension cues, stitching where visible, and roughness variation tied to handling. Emissive accents must arise from a lens, strip, screen, projector, fixture, biological organ, or energy component. Do not paint unexplained neon lines across ordinary structure. Avoid the town-specific failures: citywide neon wash, toy-town proportions, sterile empty streets. Surface variation should follow manufacturing, age, handling, weather, moisture, heat, pressure, preparation, cleaning, or maintenance rather than random noise. Emissive areas must originate from a real lens, screen, fixture, projector, biological organ, or energy system.

Condition and environmental integration: Apply restrained lived-in wear at contact points, lower edges, hinges, handles, feet, fasteners, drainage paths, service openings, tires, exposed corners, or frequently cleaned surfaces. Match the district’s maintenance level rather than using uniform dirt or uniform perfection. Place it on a named ground, wall, ceiling, counter, shelf, dock, room, vehicle, terrain, water, or gameplay socket appropriate to its use. Every foot, base, root, bracket, anchor, contact edge, and suspension point must sit flush or visibly explain how it is supported. Add contact shadows, foundations, feet, brackets, roots, piles, seals, trim, drainage, terrain blending, waterline response, or wall transitions where the object meets its environment. It may not appear pasted into the scene or suspended by invisible support unless the design explicitly includes a justified force, mount, cable, lift field, or suspension system.

Interaction and state design: Separate parts that may open, rotate, light, display, receive an item, emit particles, take damage, change material, or connect to another system. Expected hooks include transform, material-state, damage, pickup, or placement hook only where gameplay requires it. Separate and name parts that can open, slide, rotate, illuminate, display content, receive an item, carry an occupant, change material, emit particles, take damage, be repaired, be harvested, or connect to another system. Static detail should remain efficient, but useful gameplay state boundaries may not be merged away.

Collision, orientation, and export: Use one or more primitive or low-complexity hulls matching the major blocking volume and interaction surface. Decorative handles, cables, slats, fasteners, trim, lenses, foliage, and surface detail must not create snagging collision. Use positive Z as the front or primary use direction and positive Y as up after export conversion. Place the origin at the ground contact, wall mount, suspension point, waterline, or logical placement center. Use one named asset root, semantically named render meshes, separate animated or stateful parts, simplified collision, and metadata for asset ID, town, family, source document, license, dimensions, final semantic category, and specification version. Remove preview cameras, lights, helpers, unused materials, duplicates, hidden placeholders, and accidental geometry before GLB export.

Performance and LOD: Preserve silhouette and interaction points, sharing repeated hardware and moving only microdetail into materials at lower LODs. Close-range output may use up to the reviewed maximum, with a practical target near 23,400 triangles when silhouette and required components justify it. Medium-range output should target roughly 10,800 triangles while preserving primary form, supports, interaction components, openings, material blocks, and essential lights. Far output should target roughly 3,600 triangles or a suitable impostor while retaining the recognizable outline, mounting or ground relationship, and major color or emissive signature. Reduction may never destroy this recognition requirement: The primary body and functional secondary parts must identify the object before labels or color. Handles, supports, openings, controls, edges, and contact points should explain use.

Acceptance standard: the final model must look intentional from every inspection angle, satisfy every required component, fit the reviewed scale, use meaningful material separation, remain inside geometry budgets, sit correctly on its placement plane, and export as a verified nonempty GLB. A technically valid file that looks generic, toy-like, structurally impossible, context-free, semantically misclassified, or unlike Starter Retaining Wall is a failure. Correct it, retry it, or quarantine it instead of publishing it.

Keep the working envelope near 1.5 meters wide, 1.5 meters deep, and 1.5 meters high. Only reviewed protrusions such as signs, arms, doors, mirrors, roots, branches, railings, hoses, lighting, propulsion, awnings, stairs, or service hardware may extend beyond it. Every major and secondary form must reinforce Starter Wood Fence; unrelated decorative mass should be removed.

Construction and functional anatomy: Include mounting, foundations or brackets, structural members, weather or pressure protection, access, hinges, latches, vents, conduit or cable paths, drainage, warnings, controls, and maintenance hardware as appropriate. Required visible components are recognizable primary structure, functional secondary components, appropriate materials. Each one must connect through credible frames, joints, seams, foundations, roots, brackets, fasteners, cables, pipes, glazing frames, hinges, biological attachment, serving structure, packaging, or material transitions. Flat paint, decals, and emission may not replace a component that explains operation, weight support, access, occupancy, growth, containment, drainage, power, preparation, protection, or maintenance.

Materials, color, and lighting: use the named material vocabulary painted metal, concrete, ordinary glass, galvanized hardware, warm brick, cream, storefront blue, civic navy, school green, utility gray, residential sage. welcoming, lived-in American city realism; warm brick, stucco, concrete, patched asphalt, painted metal, ordinary civic and residential materials. Metal surfaces need distinct painted, powder-coated, galvanized, brushed, cast, polished, oxidized, or heat-affected responses rather than one universal gray material. Stone, brick, concrete, plaster, stucco, tile, and asphalt should show scale-correct joints, aggregate or surface breakup, edge wear, drainage staining, and construction transitions without noisy procedural speckling. Wood needs believable board direction, grain scale, end grain, joinery, sealing, wear, and moisture response appropriate to indoor, residential, marine, fantasy, or industrial use. Fabric, upholstery, leather, rubber, and flexible polymers require thickness, seams, compression or tension cues, stitching where visible, and roughness variation tied to handling. Emissive accents must arise from a lens, strip, screen, projector, fixture, biological organ, or energy component. Do not paint unexplained neon lines across ordinary structure. Separate and name parts that can open, slide, rotate, illuminate, display content, receive an item, carry an occupant, change material, emit particles, take damage, be repaired, be harvested, or connect to another system. Static detail should remain efficient, but useful gameplay state boundaries may not be merged away.

Collision, orientation, and export: Use one or more primitive or low-complexity hulls matching the major blocking volume and interaction surface. Decorative handles, cables, slats, fasteners, trim, lenses, foliage, and surface detail must not create snagging collision. Use positive Z as the front or primary use direction and positive Y as up after export conversion. Place the origin at the ground contact, wall mount, suspension point, waterline, or logical placement center. Use one named asset root, semantically named render meshes, separate animated or stateful parts, simplified collision, and metadata for asset ID, town, family, source document, license, dimensions, final semantic category, and specification version. Remove preview cameras, lights, helpers, unused materials, duplicates, hidden placeholders, and accidental geometry before GLB export.

Performance and LOD: Preserve functional outline, installation, and operating surfaces. Repeated bolts, louvers, bars, lenses, posts, and rails should use instancing, while collision follows major volumes. Close-range output may use up to the reviewed maximum, with a practical target near 23,400 triangles when silhouette and required components justify it. Medium-range output should target roughly 10,800 triangles while preserving primary form, supports, interaction components, openings, material blocks, and essential lights. Far output should target roughly 3,600 triangles or a suitable impostor while retaining the recognizable outline, mounting or ground relationship, and major color or emissive signature. Reduction may never destroy this recognition requirement: Recognition must come from the relationship between support, enclosure, operating surface, access point, protected hardware, and ground, wall, dock, road, or network connection.

Acceptance standard: the final model must look intentional from every inspection angle, satisfy every required component, fit the reviewed scale, use meaningful material separation, remain inside geometry budgets, sit correctly on its placement plane, and export as a verified nonempty GLB. Correct it, retry it, or quarantine it instead of publishing it.

productionBrief.placement: Place it on a named floor, wall, counter, workstation, classroom, bedroom, shop, restaurant, sanitary, storage, or service socket. Feet, wall brackets, plumbing, cable routes, backs, and user clearance must align with the room and nearby interaction positions.
productionBrief.silhouetteAndProportion: Seat or work height, depth, back angle, leg clearance, storage volume, support placement, and reachable controls must immediately explain how a person uses the object.
productionBrief.structuralConstruction: Model load-bearing frames, legs, pedestals, brackets, seams, cushions, panels, drawers, hinges, plumbing, glides, cable routing, fasteners, wall anchors, or floor anchors appropriate to the item.

materialPlan.metalRule: Metal surfaces need distinct painted, powder-coated, galvanized, brushed, cast, polished, oxidized, or heat-affected responses rather than one universal gray material.
materialPlan.glassRule: Glass requires thickness, framing, tint appropriate to the town, controlled transparency, believable roughness, and an interior or backing surface so it does not read as an empty blue plane.
materialPlan.masonryRule: Stone, brick, concrete, plaster, stucco, tile, and asphalt should show scale-correct joints, aggregate or surface breakup, edge wear, drainage staining, and construction transitions without noisy procedural speckling.
materialPlan.woodRule: Wood needs believable board direction, grain scale, end grain, joinery, sealing, wear, and moisture response appropriate to indoor, residential, marine, fantasy, or industrial use.
materialPlan.flexibleRule: Fabric, upholstery, leather, rubber, and flexible polymers require thickness, seams, compression or tension cues, stitching where visible, and roughness variation tied to handling.
materialPlan.emissiveRule: Emissive accents must arise from a lens, strip, screen, projector, fixture, biological organ, or energy component. Do not paint unexplained neon lines across ordinary structure.

townArtDirection.style: welcoming, lived-in American city realism; warm brick, stucco, concrete, patched asphalt, painted metal, ordinary civic and residential materials

productionBrief.conditionAndWear: Apply restrained lived-in wear at contact points, lower edges, hinges, handles, feet, fasteners, drainage paths, service openings, tires, exposed corners, or frequently cleaned surfaces. Match the district’s maintenance level rather than using uniform dirt or uniform perfection.

interactionAndAnimation.guidance: Preserve seats, drawers, doors, screens, lamps, cushions, controls, storage, plumbing fixtures, and movable surfaces as distinct objects when gameplay can sit, open, use, move, customize, or damage them.
hooks: transform, material-state, damage, pickup, or placement hook only where gameplay requires it

productionBrief.collision: Use one or more primitive or low-complexity hulls matching the major blocking volume and interaction surface. Decorative handles, cables, slats, fasteners, trim, lenses, foliage, and surface detail must not create snagging collision.
productionBrief.orientationAndPivot: Use positive Z as the front or primary use direction and positive Y as up after export conversion. Place the origin at the ground contact, wall mount, suspension point, waterline, or logical placement center.
productionBrief.optimization: Keep ergonomic silhouette and contact points at every LOD. Repeated slats, legs, buttons, cushions, shelves, and fasteners should share meshes or instances.

Physical identity and semantic decision: the final category is road_surface because strong filename prefix resolves the physical object as road_surface. Model it as a modular traversal, road, sidewalk, bridge, dock, platform, path, rail, or course asset designed to connect cleanly and support movement without floating or snagging geometry. Words describing an animal, profession, customer, owner, district, collection, or story function may not force character or creature anatomy onto an object such as a cottage, boat, crate, display, station, rack, board, feeder, machine, sign, or piece of equipment. The named object must be identifiable in neutral clay material before labels, color, and glow are applied.

Silhouette and proportion: Edge profile, grade, lane or path width, curb or barrier, structural support, connection points, and travel direction must explain how the surface carries players or vehicles. Keep the working envelope near 10 meters wide, 10 meters deep, and 0.3 meters high. Only reviewed protrusions such as signs, arms, doors, mirrors, roots, branches, railings, hoses, lighting, propulsion, awnings, stairs, or service hardware may extend beyond it. Every major and secondary form must reinforce Starter Alley; unrelated decorative mass should be removed.

Construction and functional anatomy: Provide surface thickness, engineered edges, joints, drainage, markings, supports, retaining structure, barriers, and transition pieces. Elevated or marine modules require believable beams, columns, cables, piles, brackets, or anchors. Required visible components are surface slab, curbs or edges, lane or path markings, connection seams, drainage detail. Each one must connect through credible frames, joints, seams, foundations, roots, brackets, fasteners, cables, pipes, glazing frames, hinges, biological attachment, serving structure, packaging, or material transitions. Flat paint, decals, and emission may not replace a component that explains operation, weight support, access, occupancy, growth, containment, drainage, power, preparation, protection, or maintenance.

Materials, color, and lighting: use the named material vocabulary painted metal, concrete, ordinary glass, galvanized hardware, warm brick, cream, storefront blue, civic navy, school green, utility gray, residential sage. welcoming, lived-in American city realism; warm brick, stucco, concrete, patched asphalt, painted metal, ordinary civic and residential materials. Stone, brick, concrete, plaster, stucco, tile, and asphalt should show scale-correct joints, aggregate or surface breakup, edge wear, drainage staining, and construction transitions without noisy procedural speckling. Wood needs believable board direction, grain scale, end grain, joinery, sealing, wear, and moisture response appropriate to indoor, residential, marine, fantasy, or industrial use. Fabric, upholstery, leather, rubber, and flexible polymers require thickness, seams, compression or tension cues, stitching where visible, and roughness variation tied to handling. Emissive accents must arise from a lens, strip, screen, projector, fixture, biological organ, or energy component. Do not paint unexplained neon lines across ordinary structure. Avoid the town-specific failures: citywide neon wash, toy-town proportions, sterile empty streets. Surface variation should follow manufacturing, age, handling, weather, moisture, heat, pressure, preparation, cleaning, or maintenance rather than random noise. Emissive areas must originate from a real lens, screen, fixture, projector, biological organ, or energy system.

Condition and environmental integration: Apply restrained lived-in wear at contact points, lower edges, hinges, handles, feet, fasteners, drainage paths, service openings, tires, exposed corners, or frequently cleaned surfaces. Match the district’s maintenance level rather than using uniform dirt or uniform perfection. Snap it to the road, path, bridge, dock, rail, platform, course, or terrain grid with exact edge continuity, matching elevation, consistent width, correct travel direction, believable support spacing, and continuous simplified collision. No gaps, overlaps, floating ends, or invisible ledges are allowed. Add contact shadows, foundations, feet, brackets, roots, piles, seals, trim, drainage, terrain blending, waterline response, or wall transitions where the object meets its environment. It may not appear pasted into the scene or suspended by invisible support unless the design explicitly includes a justified force, mount, cable, lift field, or suspension system.

Interaction and state design: Define walk, drive, climb, jump, grind, checkpoint, hazard, fall, docking, and connection boundaries through named surfaces and sockets. Expected hooks include transform, material-state, damage, pickup, or placement hook only where gameplay requires it. Separate and name parts that can open, slide, rotate, illuminate, display content, receive an item, carry an occupant, change material, emit particles, take damage, be repaired, be harvested, or connect to another system. Static detail should remain efficient, but useful gameplay state boundaries may not be merged away.

Collision, orientation, and export: Use continuous simplified traversal collision matching grades, gaps, curbs, rails, docking edges, fall boundaries, and platform surfaces. Decorative cracks, bolts, grates, trim, and surface noise must not create snagging micro-collision. Use positive Z as the travel or module-continuation direction and positive Y as up after export conversion. Place the origin at the documented grid center, connection edge, spline point, or docking plane. Use one named asset root, semantically named render meshes, separate animated or stateful parts, simplified collision, and metadata for asset ID, town, family, source document, license, dimensions, final semantic category, and specification version. Remove preview cameras, lights, helpers, unused materials, duplicates, hidden placeholders, and accidental geometry before GLB export.

Performance and LOD: Use modular dimensions, shared materials, and continuous simplified collision. Distant LODs may reduce cracks and hardware but cannot change grade, gaps, width, edge safety, or traversal timing. Close-range output may use up to the reviewed maximum, with a practical target near 7,800 triangles when silhouette and required components justify it. Medium-range output should target roughly 3,600 triangles while preserving primary form, supports, interaction components, openings, material blocks, and essential lights. Far output should target roughly 1,200 triangles or a suitable impostor while retaining the recognizable outline, mounting or ground relationship, and major color or emissive signature. Reduction may never destroy this recognition requirement: Edge profile, grade, lane or path width, curb or barrier, structural support, connection points, and travel direction must explain how the surface carries players or vehicles.

Acceptance standard: the final model must look intentional from every inspection angle, satisfy every required component, fit the reviewed scale, use meaningful material separation, remain inside geometry budgets, sit correctly on its placement plane, and export as a verified nonempty GLB. A technically valid file that looks generic, toy-like, structurally impossible, context-free, semantically misclassified, or unlike Starter Alley is a failure. Correct it, retry it, or quarantine it instead of publishing it.

Keep the working envelope near 10 meters wide, 10 meters deep, and 0.3 meters high. Required visible components are surface slab, curbs or edges, lane or path markings, connection seams, drainage detail. Each one must connect through credible frames, joints, seams, foundations, roots, brackets, fasteners, cables, pipes, glazing frames, hinges, biological attachment, serving structure, packaging, or material transitions. Metal surfaces need distinct painted, powder-coated, galvanized, brushed, cast, polished, oxidized, or heat-affected responses rather than one universal gray material. Fabric, upholstery, leather, rubber, and flexible polymers require thickness, seams, compression or tension cues, stitching where visible, and roughness variation tied to handling. Expected hooks include transform, material-state, damage, pickup, or placement hook only where gameplay requires it. Place the origin at the documented grid center, connection edge, spline point, or docking plane. Remove preview cameras, lights, helpers, unused materials, duplicates, hidden placeholders, and accidental geometry before GLB export.

Acceptance standard: the final model must look intentional from every inspection angle, satisfy every required component, fit the reviewed scale, use meaningful material separation, remain inside geometry budgets, sit correctly on its placement plane, and export as a verified nonempty GLB.
